projects.title: CashDB-lite: A Leaderless Quorum KV Store with Deterministic Simulation Testing
projects.pitch: Build a small leaderless replicated key-value store using ABD majority quorums, then build a deterministic simulator that injects partitions, delays and crashes from a seed. The simulator checks every history for linearizability, so you can prove the store is correct rather than assume it. Once ABD passes, add a single-key compare-and-swap path and watch latency degrade under contention, which is the weakness the talk describes.
stack: Rust 1.100 (DropGuard for rollback on aborted ops, never type in the error paths)
tokio, swappable for a seeded single-threaded simulated runtime
Porcupine-style linearizability checker (port or write your own)
sled or plain append-only files for replica storage
you_will_learn: Majority quorum intersection and why ABD reads need a write-back phase
Linearizability vs. eventual consistency, checked mechanically on real histories
Deterministic simulation testing: controlling time, randomness and network from one seed
Replica catch-up, read repair and the cost of contention on leaderless writes
Designing I/O behind traits so production and simulated runtimes share one code path
milestones: Single-node store with versioned (timestamp, node_id) registers behind a Network/Clock/Storage trait boundary
3- and 5-replica ABD reads and writes over a real TCP transport
Seeded simulator that injects message drops, reordering, partitions and node restarts, with failing seeds reproducible
History recorder plus linearizability checker; break the write-back phase on purpose and confirm the checker catches it
Read repair and anti-entropy catch-up for a replica returning after a long partition
Add CAS, benchmark p50/p99 under rising key contention, and write up how this motivates EPaxos or Accord

projects.title: Mini-Datacat: An OpenTelemetry Ingest Pipeline with Backpressure into ClickHouse
projects.pitch: Write an OTLP/HTTP receiver that accepts traces, metrics and logs from instrumented demo services. Batch the data into ClickHouse through a bounded pipeline that degrades predictably under load. Then put a small query API and an alerting loop on top. The interesting part is not the dashboards. It is what happens when ingest outruns the database.
stack: Go or Rust OTLP receiver (protobuf over HTTP)
ClickHouse (MergeTree tables, TTLs, materialized views)
OpenTelemetry SDKs in 2-3 toy services that emit load
k6 or vegeta for load generation
A tiny Grafana or HTML dashboard for the query API
you_will_learn: Backpressure: bounded queues, load shedding, and returning 429/503 with Retry-After the way OTLP clients expect
Batching tradeoffs: flush on size vs. time, and the latency/throughput curve
Columnar schema design: sort keys, partitioning, and TTL-based retention
Pre-aggregation with materialized views vs. querying raw spans
Observing the observability system itself (meta-metrics for queue depth, drop rate, flush latency)
milestones: Accept OTLP traces and write them row-by-row to ClickHouse; measure how badly that performs
Add a bounded in-memory queue with size/time batch flushing and measure the improvement
Implement load shedding plus OTLP-compliant retry signaling; run a load test that exceeds capacity and verify no OOM
Design span and metric tables with sensible ORDER BY keys; add 1-minute rollups via materialized views
Query API for trace lookup by ID, service latency percentiles, and error-rate time series
Alert evaluator with for-duration semantics and deduplication; document a capacity plan

projects.title: Port-the-5%: Profile-Guided Rust Extensions with Differential Equivalence Proofs
projects.pitch: Take a deliberately slow Python service, such as a log parser, a fuzzy matcher, or a geo-distance ranker. Profile it to find the hot functions. Port only those to Rust via PyO3, and prove the port behaves identically using property-based differential testing against the original. The deliverable is a speedup report backed by evidence, not just a faster binary.
stack: Python 3.13 with py-spy and scalene for profiling
Rust + PyO3 + maturin
Hypothesis (Python) for differential property tests
pytest-benchmark or hyperfine
Optional: a coding agent to draft the port, which you then verify
you_will_learn: Reading flamegraphs and separating CPU-bound, allocation-bound and I/O-bound hotspots
Amdahl's law in practice: why porting 5% of the code can yield large or negligible wins
FFI boundary costs: GIL release, data marshalling, and zero-copy buffers
Differential testing and edge-case semantics (Unicode, float rounding, integer overflow)
Building a reproducible benchmark harness that can't fool you
milestones: Build or pick a realistic slow Python app and capture baseline flamegraphs under a fixed workload
Rank hotspots and predict the end-to-end speedup with Amdahl's law before writing any Rust
Port the top function with PyO3; release the GIL where safe
Differential Hypothesis suite comparing Python and Rust outputs across millions of generated inputs; fix the divergences it finds
Measure FFI overhead and restructure calls to batch across the boundary
Write a report comparing predicted vs. actual speedup, the semantic differences found, and the remaining hotspots

projects.title: Contract Gate: Enforcing ODCS Data Contracts on a Streaming Pipeline
projects.pitch: Build a producer-to-consumer event pipeline with a contract gate in between. The gate validates every batch against an Open Data Contract Standard YAML file covering schema, semantic quality rules and freshness SLAs. Violating records go to a dead-letter store, and contract versions evolve safely. Finally, expose the contracts over an endpoint so an AI agent consumer can discover what the data means before using it.
stack: Python or TypeScript
ODCS v3 YAML contracts
Redpanda or NATS JetStream for the event stream
DuckDB or Postgres as the consumer warehouse
JSON Schema plus SQL-based quality checks
you_will_learn: Schema evolution: backward and forward compatibility rules, and detecting breaking changes in CI
Treating datasets as APIs with provider-driven, versioned interfaces
Dead-letter queues, quarantine and replay semantics
Freshness and completeness SLAs as measurable signals with alerts
Machine-readable metadata for autonomous consumers
milestones: Producer emits order events; consumer loads them into DuckDB with no contract (baseline)
Write an ODCS contract; the gate validates schema and rejects bad records to a DLQ with reasons attached
Add quality rules (ranges, uniqueness, referential checks) and freshness SLA monitoring
Contract diff tool that classifies a version change as breaking or non-breaking and fails CI on unannounced breaks
Run v1 and v2 contracts side by side with consumer-pinned versions, then do a migration drill
Contract discovery endpoint; let an LLM agent answer questions using only contract metadata and compare its accuracy with and without it

projects.title: Attested Key Release: A Zero-Operator-Access Toy with a Merkle Transparency Log
projects.pitch: Recreate Bee's architecture in miniature. A workload VM measures its boot chain and container image into a software TPM. A key broker releases a short-lived, in-memory-only decryption key only when the attestation quote matches an expected measurement published in an append-only Merkle transparency log. Clients verify inclusion proofs before trusting anything.
stack: swtpm + tpm2-tools (software TPM, no cloud required)
Go or Rust for the key broker and attestation verifier
Your own Merkle-tree log (RFC 6962 style), with Sigstore Rekor as an optional comparison
QEMU or a container to stand in for the attested workload
mTLS with the attestation evidence embedded in a certificate extension
you_will_learn: Measured boot and PCR extend semantics: why measurements chain and can't be rolled back
Remote attestation: quotes, nonces for freshness, and replay prevention
Merkle trees: inclusion and consistency proofs, and detecting a log that rewrites history
Short-lived credentials, key rotation, and keeping secrets off disk
Threat modeling: which risks attestation covers and which need network isolation or separation of duties
milestones: Use swtpm to extend PCRs with hashes of a boot script, container image and model file; produce a signed quote
Append-only Merkle log service with inclusion and consistency proof endpoints, plus a client-side verifier
Key broker that verifies quote signature, nonce freshness and PCR values against logged expectations, then issues a 5-minute key
Embed attestation evidence in an mTLS cert so clients verify before sending data
Attack drills: tampered image, replayed quote, forked log; each must be detected
Write a threat-model doc covering what is protected, what isn't, and which operational controls fill the gaps
